methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective cohort 5,052 breast cancer patients from single hospital (2004-2024). Logistic regression modeling discharge status. Limitations: single-center, hospitalized patients only (outpatients not captured), short-term outcomes (discharge status not long-term survival), missing molecular subtype data.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Descriptive epidemiologic analysis of inpatient breast cancer management evolution. Limited clinical utility for individual patient decisions. Relevant for healthcare administration and resource allocation at institutional level.

reporting_quality.justification: Methods describe retrospective design and data source (hospital administrative system). Results present demographic, clinical, and treatment patterns. Lacks molecular subtype data acknowledged as limitation. Data availability not discussed.

novelty_literature.justification: Confirms known epidemiologic patterns (peak age 40-59, upper outer quadrant predominance). Trend analysis adds minimal novelty; no mechanistic insights or practice-changing findings.

writing_presentation.justification: Clear organization of demographic, clinical, treatment data. Figures effectively show temporal trends (LOS reduction, cost evolution). Some repetition in context sections.

key_strengths: Large single-institution cohort (5,052 patients) with 20-year observation period
Comprehensive demographic and clinical characteristic documentation
Clear presentation of temporal trends in surgical management and costs
key_concerns: Purely descriptive analysis without comparison group or causal inference mechanisms
Selection bias: hospitalized patients only; outpatient management not captured
Short-term outcomes only (discharge status); long-term survival and recurrence unavailable
Missing molecular subtype data fundamentally limits interpretation of treatment patterns
chief_reviewer.rationale: Comprehensive retrospective trend analysis documenting regional breast cancer management. Limited novelty; confirms established epidemiologic patterns. Lack of long-term outcomes and molecular data, combined with purely descriptive design, falls below publication threshold for peer-reviewed oncology journals.
